utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, you're to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning to you and to Your Honours. I have just one final question in response to His Honour Judge Mindua's question yesterday to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Cannata [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't hear you. I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That is being looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: May I suggest, while we're trying to fix this problem, to load Exhibit P308, which is the map, as marked yesterday from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's see if the channel problem with the interpretation for the witness is solved.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It has been resolved, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take you back to the map you marked yesterday, and I wish you to clarify the answer you gave to His Honour Judge Mindua to the question about how you establish or how you assume that the shell fell on Bascarsija. Now, let me ask you this: You gave yesterday evidence that you were -- you were located at the place which is marked with the letter A in the map; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which direction were you walking to when you heard the shell being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Brajkovac area which means I was moving towards the trenches, towards the front line, in other words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, roughly, you were going south in the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we can say that Bascarsija was on your back and Vidikovac in diagonal with respect to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bascarsija was to my right at the time. I was heading for the Brajkovac area and then Bascarsija would have been to my right, from the place where I was at the time. The Trebevic area would have been to my left then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So we can say that -- let me put it this way: With respect to your position which was the direction from where you heard the sound of the shell being fired? Was it on the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to my left; in the direction of Vidikovac, up there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And, again, with respect to the position you had at the time, which direction you heard the sound coming from of the shell exploding? Was it the right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, well, you can't put the answer to him. You shouldn't put the answer, just ask him the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was on my right-hand side; from my right flank, as it were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How long was the period of time between the sound of the shell being fired you heard and the sound of the shell exploding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took a very brief time, a second or two, several seconds; no more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the direction of the sound of the shell being fired along with the direction of the sound of the shell exploding and the fact that there was a short period of time between the two sounds, would those factors might have assisted you in assuming that the shell fell on Bascarsija that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those are the only factors. The time between the sound of the shell being fired and the shell exploding was very short, several seconds perhaps; and that led to us conclude that the shell had been fired from Vidikovac and had landed in the Bascarsija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further question, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I represent the accused, Dragomir Milosevic. My name is Branislav Tapuskovic. I, too, would like to ask you some questions so that we might clarify everything that you have been talking about. The one thing I'd like to ask you is please try to keep your answers as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My first question: Can you confirm what you have already talked about. From the beginning of the conflict and even several months after the conflict had ended, you had been a soldier of the BH army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. From June 1992 to sometime after Dayton, back in 1996. It might have been April, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Just to remind my learned friend from the Defence that he has to switch the microphone off when the witness is to talk for protections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The 115th Brigade that you were a member of -- you see, I have to focus my questions on the time-period between August 1994 and the 21st of November, 1995. Do you understand me, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Indeed. But the 1st Corps comprised three divisions, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You spent the entire war in the conflict, and you don't know about the three divisions belonging to the BH army, the 1st Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, sir. I know that I belonged to the 115th Brigade, and I know that I belonged to the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you still don't know whether at the time in question your brigade belonged to the 12th division of the 1st Corps of the BH army, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Believe me, this is the very first I hear of it. I couldn't even say I was interested in that sort of thing at the time. When the war eventually ended, I was glad to finally see the war end. I left the army as a civilian, which was sometime in mid-April 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't know that the two divisions of the 1st Corps were outside Sarajevo at other positions elsewhere, Igman and another place as well, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that. I know that certain units would go outside Sarajevo. As for the divisions you mention, I'm not sure what you mean when you say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the time in question, the 1st Corps of the BH army was transformed into three divisions; the 12th, the 14th, and the 16th. Are you telling me you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that there were units belonging to the 1st Corps that you were outside Sarajevo, don't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. Even my own unit would sometimes leave Sarajevo itself and stay away for as long as a month. Our area of responsibility was in the area of the Nisic plateau, but we were still part of the brigade. We remained part of the brigade, not part of the Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the area of responsibility of the 115th Brigade? You would leave Sarajevo through the tunnel that existed under the airport; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you use this map, the one behind us, please, and show us, first of all, where the tunnel was; and, secondly, once you cross the tunnel, where exactly would you get to? Where is the Nisic plateau?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may not be able to be perfectly accurate, but I know that it was somewhere in the Dobrinja area that one ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. Will the witness take his seat. Witness, take your seat. We have to go into private session. We have to go into private session if the witness is going to leave his seat.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, I'm facing a problem concerning my exhibit list. As early as the 28th of February, as early as the 28th of February, I submitted all the exhibits that I was going to use in relation to this witness. I have learned from the OTP that some of my documents DD00-1015 and 113 and 117, that they didn't receive those. I put that into e-court as early as the 28th; therefore, I'm at a loss as to why those documents are now missing from my list. One of these documents is essential in relation to this very question, that the witness is trying to answer DD00-10113 [as interpreted]. Can we please first try to retrieve that document, because I have submitted the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're referring to DD00-0105?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-1013; but it's not in e-court. I'm not sure where the glitch occurred. It's not today that I submitted this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us hear from the court deputy whether it can be retrieved.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have been told that the Defence can now release the document. It's in their basket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You heard that, Mr. Tapuskovic. What is the position? You still can't retrieve it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: An e-court technician has been summoned to see if the problem can be resolved. In the meantime, let us resort to the ancient, well-tried, and tested system. Do you have the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do. I can show it to the witness. The witness can have a look, and after that I can read out portions of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us do that and move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You have it on the screen now. Can you see that, Witness?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order dated the 11th of July, 1995. The order is in reference to your brigade as well. You can see that on the right-hand side. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was just an ordinary soldier. This is not the kind of order that was ever read out to me. I would up sticks and leave with my unit whenever the unit received any orders, normally. In fact, I spent a total of nine months elsewhere outside Sarajevo, specifically at the Nisic plateau along the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber is a bit in the dark here. Could you please share with us the information as to who issued this order and who was it issued to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order issued to the commands, the command of his brigade, too. That is on the right-hand side, and it was issued by the commander of the 12th division, Trebevic. I got this from the BH army archive. I do understand that as an ordinary soldier, the witness is not necessarily familiar with this. I would like to tell him what it is about despite that, and I would like to ask him whether he was involved in what appears to the substance of this order. I believe he has never seen the order, but I would like to know if he ever acted in accordance and in the spirit of this order, as he must have been ordered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you first; you spent as many as nine months outside the area of the responsibility of the 115th Brigade, in other areas outside of Sarajevo itself. You say you never saw an 120-millimetre mortar in your own area. Did you ever see it anywhere else in Sarajevo or outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not along my own line of responsibility; not once. A while ago you said outside the area covered by my brigade; whenever we left Sarajevo. That, too, was the area of responsibility of my brigade; I mean the Nisic plateau, among other areas. That, too, was included.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Nisic plateau is far away, far away from Sarajevo, outside Sarajevo in a different area. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. But probably that area, too, fell under my brigade. That was another one of our defence sectors, and that is the only way I can explain it. We started leaving the city sometime in mid-1993 and then we continued from there on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly at the time in question, right, the time that I specified to you between the 10th of August 1994 at the end -- and the end of the war. Is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean 1994 or 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From August 1994 to the 21st of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was still with this unit of the 115th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll read the order to you, and I would like to ask you whether you acted in the spirit of this order. "With the aim of changing shifts of units of the battalion of the 12th Division and the resubordinated command of the 16th Division, and also with the objective of taking all the measures necessary to prepare and organise units for taking over their shifts, I hereby order. Brigade command shall immediately take all necessary measures and prepare the units of the battalions to relieve those other units in the area of responsibility of the 16th Division." Is this something that you know anything about, since you were transferred outside Sarajevo to a different area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But I know nothing about this. This is the very first time I have ever seen this order, and I know nothing about it. I do know that we sometimes left Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, if the microphone from the Defence would be switched off when the witness is speaking, because it's really important to enforce the measure of voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have a copy of this document, and on our screens it was entirely illegible; therefore, we cannot vouch for the accuracy of our interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have heard that, and for the second time, you have been cautioned, Mr. Tapuskovic. So please see that your microphone is turned off when it is supposed to be turned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I have to do that, but I'm not a machine myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see towards the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's very important that it be done, and I will not accept what appears to be a casual attitude towards it. If you can't do it, then ask your -- your manager to see that it is turned off when it should be turned off.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you're absolutely right. I'm not trying to excuse myself. It does happen; I can't help it. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, look at item 4 here. It says that "the 115th Battalion of the Mountain Brigade of Sarajevo will come on the 18th of May." Does that involve your movement as a member of the unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably involved our setting off from the barracks and the city, yes. I can see now that it is the 18th of July 1995, and that is the date when the unit set off; and further downwards, it says that we will set off at 2100 hours. As I said, we had to go through the tunnel during night-time, due to shelling and everything else that was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You already mentioned what is said in the next paragraph, and here it says, "As far as facility D-B," did you know anything about this code, that this was the code referring to the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. We just knew that there was a tunnel and that was the only way out of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you leave the city and the area of responsibility of the 115th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight times, and I spent nine months deployed outside of the town; a little bit less than nine months.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in these areas of deployment, you took part in combat operations against the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, not against the army of Republika Srpska. I was only defending my positions from the army of Republika Srpska, not against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you reached this Nisic plateau, this is very, very far away from Sarajevo, and the area of responsibility of the 115th Brigade. You weren't there in order to participate in the operations where -- in the area where you arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you think that Nisic Visoravan was not in Bosnia-Herzegovina? I was a member of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I know very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How far is Nisic from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Roughly 50 kilometres down the road, but we had to go much further because we couldn't use this road. It sometimes took us two days to reach the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And when you went there, were you regularly in active combat with the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. There was already a line established there, and we just went to be deployed along this defence line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So for the duration of your stay, were you ever engaged in active combat with the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would happen that they start shooting at the lines or shelling it; and like on any other front line, you have to respond with whatever you had available and what we had was mostly small arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And what did they have?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. But I do know that there was fire from all kinds of weapons; mortars, guns, semi-automatic rifles --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Anti-aircraft guns, anti-aircraft machine guns, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's been brought to my attention that there is probably a miscatch with the interpretation. The witness, apparently, answered to the question put by my learned friend: How far is Nisic from Sarajevo? Apparently, the witness has answered 15 kilometres and not 50 as I can read in the transcript. Can we clarify this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will ask the witness. How far is Nisic from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around 50 metres. 50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: 50, 5-0. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, lest I forget, DD00- --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number of the document, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] DD00-1013. I would like to have it marked for identification, and this is the order that we have been just discussing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D98, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when you reached these areas with your brigade, were you facing the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not very familiar with this area, but I know that the lines were in front of us, or most probably towards the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, and that fire was coming from that direction. So they were -- the lines were in front of me in the area of Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The front line of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you assert that in the relevant period, in the last year of war, that the BH army was much more poorly armed than the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Very much poorly -- there's no comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since I have time concerns, let me now move on to the statements that you make, and let me begin with the statement that you gave on the 20th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's P306 exhibit, and could the witness please be shown this statement on his screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can we be sure that it's not broadcast outside?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the court deputy will see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that the statement that you gave on the 20th of November, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please look at page 2 of your statement, so that I can put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is the request of my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, still valid?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you're speaking about. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, look at the beginning of your statement: "I don't remember what the weather was on the 22nd of November, 1994." Here you spoke about the 22nd of November, 1994, and not about the 22nd December, 1995, which you mention in your second statement. How do you explain that on a -- a year later or, rather, after the incident, you spoke about the incident that happened on the 22nd of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's a mistake. It's a misprint, the 22nd of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I must tell you that I don't believe that you were able to sign such a statement containing such a mistake in the first sentence. How do you account for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that it was possible that the statement contains such a mistake in the first sentence of your statement given on that date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I look at the second statement? I think that in the second statement also reads the 22nd November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. You were not even sure about that at that time, but let me proceed with this statement. You said: "I only recall hearing shooting on my way to the front line." What kind of shooting are you talking about? From which side was it coming or was it an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was coming from one side. It was infantry fire, and it typically happened when they intended to shell. First, they would start with infantry fire to proceed with the firing of shelling, in order for us not to hear the shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. I'm still asking you about the relevant period. Was fire always coming in those days from one side only and never from the positions of BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not always. But if there was fire, mortar fire, behind the lines where we could hear them, typically, infantry fire would be open, first, in order to cover the sound of mortar fire; not always, but in most cases that happened when they wanted to resort to shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Will you please look now at paragraph 4 which reads, according to you: "According to the sound we heard, all of us were certain that the shell was fired from Vidikovac." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's the Chetnik-held position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "I do not want to involve all the Serbs by this term, by this word I mean the aggressor."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain under such circumstances what did you mean by "the aggressor"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: By this term, I was referring to all those who were shelling Sarajevo, killing women, children, and the elderly and everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the other side of the front line, who was there? Were those your erstwhile neighbours, people who were also in their homes, or did somebody else come to that area and started shooting and shelling Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Chetniks were at the other side. Many of my neighbours stayed with me in the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We're not going to debate this any longer. Were the Chetniks the people who had been living all their lives in these areas?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were just extreme Serbs. Many Serbs stayed and remained with me in the city of Sarajevo, to defend it against those very same extreme elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is not what I'm asking. I understand what you're saying, but were those extreme Serbs local people who had been living there all their lives?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most probably, but I didn't perceive them as human beings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand your position. Let us go back now to your statement: "According to the sound, we immediately assumed that the shell was not a mortar shell, that it was probably a shell fired by a cannon because the explosion was louder than one caused by a mortar shell." Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down you said: "I can't say that I have vast experience in this matters because I was on the front line since the 26th of June, 1992." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my wartime experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it not commonly known that the sound of mortar shell -- that the intensity of the sound increases at the time of explosion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. When you fire a shell from a gun, a tank, or anything else, is much louder than a mortar shell. A mortar shell produces a kind of buffed or buffered sound when it's fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Further down on this page, several paragraphs down, it begins: "After the explosion, we heard ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "After the explosion, we heard soon after the general alert and sirens of ambulances could be heard." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Then you went on to say in the next paragraph: "After that explosion, we went to the trenches where we had our positions."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "There was just sporadic shooting on that day, and I don't recall having heard any more shells exploding." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: When you went down to the trenches, those were the trenches in Brajkovac, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't go down; we went up, because the trenches were ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long did it take you for you to go up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were not far away; probably some 50 metres diagonally.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is Brajkovac part of Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how long Debelo Brdo stretches. The line was connected to Debelo Brdo, so Brajkovac and all the rest was part of the foot of Trebevic mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that you went across Kozija Cuprija, Jarcev Dol, Dolici, Mala Colina Kapa, Velika Colina Kapa, Brajkovac, Debelo Brdo, Vranjaca, Debelo Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So that was the area of responsibility of my brigade. I couldn't cover all that in a day. We took turns. Each company or a battalion would cover it on a weekly basis; for instance, from Kozija Cuprija to Popov Gaj, then Colina Kapa, Velika, and Mala, and so on. We went around from Kozija Cuprija to Debelo Brdo, which constitutes the area of responsibility of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were those all hills overlooking Sarajevo held by BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these were just elevations, not proper hills; higher ground above the neighbourhoods of the city. And above us the units of the Republika Srpska were on the hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is exactly what I would like you to explain. Yesterday, you mentioned Vidikovac and Colina Kapa. As far as I know, Colina Kapa is 940 metres high. Can you tell me what's the difference between the height of Colina Kapa and Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly, but I believe that as the crow flies, there is between 700 and 800 metres. I cannot tell you precisely. I'm not an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the distance between these two points. I'm asking you about the difference in heights between Colina Kapa and the peak of Vidikovac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you even that either, how -- the difference between the heights, but the distance as the crow flies is about seven or 800 metres. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Both Vidikovac and Colina Kapa and even Debelo Brdo and all other elevations are part of Trebevic. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colina Kapa, Debelo Brdo were at -- are at the hill of Trebevic; however, Vidikovac was on Mount Trebevic where there was a cable car and the plateau, and that is part of Trebevic proper. Everything else was at the foot of Trebevic mountain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: From the position where your trenches were that you held and if we move onward, you come across Hrasno Brdo and Mojmilo and so on. All these hills and their ridges were held by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't go down there to the line, but I suppose that was the case. I am not sure. Actually, no, Vraca were under the control of the Serbian side; Vraca, Grbavica, and towards Hrasno Brdo. I know that these points were held by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Grbavica is downtown, isn't it? No elevations there. It's in the valley, like all other neighbourhoods in Sarajevo. What does that have to do with it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Vraca is on an elevation, above Grbavica; and then all the way to Hrasno Brdo, one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It's not my intention to dwell on this, but tell me about this. Up north, Zuc, Hum, Grdonj; I am not mentioning any other mountains?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not mountains; these are elevations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If I may just complete my question to avoid any misunderstanding. Who was in control of these elevations, the BH army, yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have to point out yet again that I never went to those lines up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us now go back to your other statement, the one dated the 20th of April, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is P307.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wish to ask you something else about the firing of that shot. Is this your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go to page 2 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, the same warning?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The court deputy will see to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the second paragraph of that statement reads: "I am unsure of the exact date of the shelling. It has been such a long time." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, sir. At the time in Sarajevo, every day was very much like any other day, and dates hardly mattered, or did the passage of time. No one kept track, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The first statement you made was back in 1995. The statement that I showed you a minute ago was given in 1995, right? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this next sentence, please. How do you explain that? "I don't know whether it was in November or December 1994." How do you explain that since you made this statement a lot later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you a while ago dates meant nothing. Days of the week meant nothing. Every day was much the same as the one before, and no one kept track of the dates and days of the week, and that was the last thing we cared to think about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. In the next paragraph you say you arrived at Brajkovac; and then you go on to state this: "I remember that we changed the shift early in the day because of the threat of snipers on the heights above us."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We would take turns early in the morning or late in the evening, precisely because of the snipers and their firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it not a fact that the only elevation overlooking the BH army positions was Vidikovac, above Colina Kapa? In any other place, the BH army had an obvious advantage in terms of positions, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not true, sir. That's not true. The Serb army held the entire Trebevic, and Trebevic is higher up than Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But a while ago you told us that you were at Colina Kapa, the Colina Kapa is 940 metres high and it's part of Trebevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but Trebevic itself is higher than that. I am not sure which lines you are referring to, but I do know that the firing was coming from over there and on that side, from up there, even the a bob track was higher up than Colina Kapa, the observatory, too. It was all higher up than the positions in Bogosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because of the sniping. You say: "There was snipers at elevations above us." Did your brigade have any snipers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show you DD00-0682; and then let me ask you something about snipers. This is a very short document, just two or three sentences. As you can see, there's a reference here to the 14th of February, 1994. Again, this is an order issued by Brigadier Nedzad Ajnadzic, and the order states: "Because of the needs for equipment and weapons for the unit, and with the objective of competently carrying out combat operations, I hereby order all brigades shall secure the hand over and transport of three sniper rifles each to military warehouses belonging to the 1st Corps. 2, these weapons must be in full working order, both the commanders and the unit itself will personally report to me on the completion of this mission." Based on this, I'm putting it to you that your brigade did have snipers in fact. These snipers were used from the positions held by your unit. Can you answer that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen this document before. Again, it is unfamiliar. I don't know that they had any, but one thing I can tell you is that my own unit did not have a single sniper. That much I'm sure of.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can this document DD00-0682 dated the 14th of February, 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number D99, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So these were the snipers and then you say: "I do remember that the weather was bad. It was foggy and dark and our view of Bascarsija was obscured." Is that what the weather was like on that day, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably so. We weren't able to see Bascarsija down in the valley where it landed, so it was a rough assessment that we made at the time. We assessed that the shell had landed at Bascarsija, but the visibility was certainly low.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the natural phenomenon of Sarajevo? There is no other city quite like that in Europe. It is in a valley. When there is fog in the valley, you cannot see anything at all in Sarajevo, not a single house. Are you familiar with that natural phenomenon, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not the whole of Sarajevo, just part of the airport and Dobrinja, isn't it, and part of Hrasnica as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On that very day, where the shell landed, as you say, Bascarsija, the place where the shell landed, was covered by thick fog, and there was nothing you could actually see down there, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. We couldn't see Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What could you see? You just heard the sound and that was that, isn't that right? You heard the explosion, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Based on what? How could you possibly know? You didn't see a thing. How could you possibly come to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, sir, if I drop this glass on the floor, you listen to the sound it makes when it hits the floor, and you know that it didn't fall over there. You know that it fell over here. It was based on the sound of the explosion that we were able to conclude where the shell had landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There's something to be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long this took, how many seconds? How many seconds between the explosion that you heard and the moment you heard the explosion down there at Bascarsija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a very short time, very short, several seconds perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see, there's a notorious, well-known fact about this weapon that I need to share with you. The shell takes 45 seconds from the place it was fired to the place it eventually hit. Forty-five seconds, that's what it would have taken. What can you say about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that is plain wrong. I don't agree with that. It takes a lot less time than you suggest, a lot less time for a shell to reach Bascarsija. I'm no artillery expert myself, but I'm saying this based on hands-on experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is still your case that it would have taken no more than three seconds, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say three seconds. I said several seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4, halfway through, you say: "But we sent a report from the front line to our headquarters about this artillery round hitting Bascarsija, and our police later contacted us about what we heard." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How do you suddenly know what people back at headquarters are doing, since you claimed a while ago only to have been aware of the actions of the ordinary soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I say our headquarters, we sent the report there; and then probably the headquarters got in touch with the police to have them take our statements. We had those wired telephones, and we used those to contact are headquarters. They wanted us to monitor any movement by the various units, any operations that were afoot, or anything like that. So we sent the report to the headquarters, and they probably forwarded the report to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Fine. You were in a trench. I am not going back to that. But in your first statement, you say that very soon after the first explosions, you heard there were ambulances driving across town, first aid being administered to people, you heard the sounds and everything. What need could you possibly have had to report this to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand your question. What do you mean "what need"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps the police came to you. Perhaps they asked to you confirm that, did they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was based on our report; that they asked us to monitor any movement by the enemy, by the various units, any operations that were in progress, that sort of thing, and we would report on this to the headquarters down there. It's probably based on that report, that the headquarters subsequently forwarded to the police, that we were later called, having returned from the front line, to make statements as to where the shell had been fired from and had landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Each time the enemy fired a shell you would report to the headquarters about where it had been fired from in a particular exchange of fire, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not every time; it would have been impossible. There were days when thousands of shells were fired. But for the most part, we did try to make reports; a shell fired from the Vidikovac area, a shell fired from the Vraca area, and so on and so forth, all of these locations around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since you seem to know this, what was this headquarters that the report was sent to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the headquarters. I'm telling that we sent this to our own unit, to the command of my company or platoon or whatever the establishment happened to be; to the company command. And they probably sent this along, the way they normally did.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: (readacted) As for the shots being fired from Spicaste Stijena, I don't know. There was a sniping activity and all sorts of weapons being used; and then Bistrik, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: One minute, Mr. Prosecutor. [Interpretation] Just a minute, please, counsel. I'd like to put a question to the witness. On page 28 line 25, you say that on some days there were thousands of shells falling. These shells were falling on the town or on the positions of the ABiH army? That is my question. I wanted to know whether shells were falling on the town, on the buildings inhabited by civilians, or whether these were falling on ABiH positions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was normally indiscriminate. They shelled the town, they shelled the lines, they shelled all the places where there were people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I didn't have the translation in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata, you had a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It's about a possible need for redaction from the transcript. I -- actually it came to my attention that the -- there is a passage from the reading of the statement that might disclose information, which probably allowed to disclose the identity of the witness or in a way to put in danger his protections. So I would suggest, and I refer to your screen about that, to redact page 29 of today's transcript, line 10 to 23 where the witness discussed the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, could you please repeat the parts that you suggest be redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's page 29 of today's transcript, line 10 to 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, out of an abundance of caution, yes, we'll have it redacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Judge Mindua, I have to go back to what you asked. All the questions I'm asking the witness are in relation to the period of the indictment, the last year of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about those thousands of shells? You speak about this particular day. There weren't that many, really. Throughout the year, was it always the same? Was it always like it was back in 1992 and 1993? This year, too, thousands of shells falling in Sarajevo every day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were few days that year when there were no shells, and we looked forward to those days. Those were happy days. But on those days, there were shells falling; maybe not thousands on any given day, but there was shelling every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about the summer of 1995? How were the shells flying? Into Sarajevo or from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Into Sarajevo. There were many more shells flying into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Something else about your statement. You say you weren't sure whether it was November or December 1994 or 1995, but please look at paragraph 4, the beginning of paragraph 4, and that's why I have the statement in front of me. You say: "I clearly remember one shell being fired and the explosion when the shell impacted; however, I'm not sure about the other round. I do not have a clear memory of the other round." Why do you make this reference to the other round? And how can you explain -- can you explain how this other round suddenly appeared on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I was told later on that two rounds had been fired at Bascarsija. I do remember clearly the first one that was fired and landed. I'm not sure about the other one. We had to hurry back to the trenches to avoid being shelled along the front line. I don't remember this other round. I can't confirm that. I know about the first round. There wasn't that much shelling that particular morning because it was foggy, that sort of thing, so I remember the first round being fired. I can't really remember the other one, whether it was fired or not. We had to hurry back to the trenches to take cover.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Just to clear the records, the witness statement never mentioned that the witness was in doubt between November or December 1994 or 1995. The statement says November or December 1994. The year 1995 is not an option, I would say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, there is no reference to 1995. That's your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is right. I meant November or December. It was a slip of the tongue on my part, but it is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness this: Who gave you the idea of there having been a second round, the other round being fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody gave me the idea. We heard this over the radio that people had been injured. By the time I got home, one of my neighbours said, Two shells have landed on Bascarsija. People have been killed and wounded, and that's where the two shells come in. I myself don't remember there being two shells. I know about the one that came from Trebevic. Now, as to Vidikovac and that sort of thing, it was probably from somewhere around there and it landed at Bascarsija.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you're not sure whether it was in November or in December 1994; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in November 1994, but let's leave it at that. It's just an assumption. I'm 90 per cent certain that it was November 1994, but not entirely positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it's the time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you're right. We'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me ask you one more question relating to the event at Nisic plateau. Did your commander at one point, the commander of the 115th Brigade, did he got killed on the positions; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't. I don't know. No, the commander of the 115th Brigade wasn't killed at the Nisic plateau.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But the battalion commander was killed and then the units abandoned the positions without the approval of the command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked the Prosecutor's approval to show a map, which is going to be very helpful for my examination. It is not on my list, though, but it will be significant if shown to the witness. It's already been tendered as Prosecutor's Exhibit. Do you allow that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Exhibit P194.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can enlarge it so as to show the positions of the 115th Brigade. All right. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It shows accurately the positions held by the 115th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so, approximately. If this is Kozija Cuprija, yes, that would be something like that, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you said that never throughout the war you saw a 120-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't see it on my front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: These two dots, to the right of 115th Mountain Brigade, indicate, according to my information, precisely the positions of this type of mortars. Can you confirm that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot, sir. I was on the front line. What was behind me, whether there were mortars or whatever, I don't know. On the lines, where I moved, there were no mortars, or I couldn't see them, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any other heavy weapons or not, and are they marked here in this map? Can you tell me that or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see any of them on the lines. We didn't have enough ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you know very well that these heavy weapons were camouflaged, in certain situations, to prevent them from being seen by the enemy. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm telling, I don't know. I never saw a mortar or anything similar, any other heavy weapons on the line and in the area of my responsibility; not on the line that I walked along.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that regard, Your Honours, I intend to show the witness another document issued by the commander of the 12th Division. He was the commander of Sarajevo. It's dated 25th of July, 1995, DD00-0782. Can we please enlarge it a bit for the benefit of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read out to you. You see that it's dated the 23rd of July, 1995, and that it's an order issued by Fikret Prevljak. You know who Fikret Prevljak was? He was the commander of your brigade as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what he says in this order: "After inspecting the units of the 12th division, it was established that anti-aircraft defence weapons," and you know that the anti-aircraft defence is something to use to shoot at aircraft; yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And then he goes on to say that these anti-aircraft weapons that are being used to fire at targets on the ground and that they hadn't been properly constructed. It seems that he believed that these weapons and the anti-aircraft weapons should be used to fire at targets on the ground. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this order, yes. But I myself never saw this order before, and I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The order says that "firing positions constructed for firing at targets on the ground should be upgraded and fortified up to the level that they guarantee safety of gunners and enable long-term combat operations." And in the next passage, he says: "When constructing firing positions, take due care for them to be fully camouflaged." Do you see this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If you never saw mortars and any heavy weapons, was that perhaps the reason, precisely, that there was such an order in existence instructing everyone for them to be camouflaged and obscured from vision of even your combatants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you, we are talking here about anti-aircraft weapons. It could be, I'm not claiming, but I personally didn't know that there were any mortars of this kind of weapons. They could have been camouflaged, I'm not denying that, but I'm telling you that I personally know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you allow for the possibility that you don't know anything about them, precisely because it had been ordered for them to be camouflaged and not be visible for anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm telling, I don't know if they existed or not. I myself didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would kindly ask for this document to be tendered for identification as exhibit -- Defence exhibit and the number DD00-0782.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit D100, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me clarify one more thing with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In these combat operations carried out either in Sarajevo or outside of Sarajevo in Nisici, et cetera, you carried out them often in coordination with police units or MUP units.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally had no contact with or wasn't involved in any concerted actions with MUP. I was just a soldier, and I was part of my unit. I don't know whether MUP units were there or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Particularly in summer 1997 [as interpreted], in view of what was happening in that summer, do you know that everyone was involved in these operation, including MUP units, your units, and everything else that was happening in June and July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, summer 1997? Can my learned friend from the Defence clarify? Probably he referred to a different year.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter confirms that the counsel said 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What did you mean to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This order that I would like to show to the witness, and I will finish with my questioning, is another order issued on the 6th of July, 1995 by Fikret Prevljak, which particularly refers to the period for which General Milosevic is accused of; that is the order date of the 6th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So it's 1995 not 1997. You said 1997. That's why the Prosecutor got to his feet. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies. The order says -- oh, no. I first have to call it up. It's DD00-0725. It's Defence exhibit. It's a very short order, another order issued by Fikret Prevljak, the commander of the 12th Division, which reads as follows: "In view of the prevailing situation on the battlefield," and I'm going to read further on, "I hereby issue the follow order. MUP units shall continue to be engaged in the areas of responsibility of the 155th, 102nd, and 105th Mountain Brigades, and the 111 VBBR. They are going to be used for defence and for securing the area of responsibility of the brigade and the airport as a vital facility in the city of Sarajevo." You know that MUP was often participating in actions, together with the BH army. You can see here that your adjacent brigades were engaged; 155, 102nd, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's no mention of my brigade. I don't know how many times I have to repeat. I don't know anything about it. I know that they were not cooperating with my brigade. Whether they were engaged in action with other brigades, I don't know about that. As for the position of my brigade, they were never involved in actions together with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is whether you're going accept this document for identification as Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Just one or two -- putting the transcript -- actually, this document was not in the list. I mean, it's not a problem. I just wanted to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: For identification. Yes, we'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, sorry. I have just been told that we already tendered this document with the witness Vidovic, so it's already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Very well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have finished my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness, did you serve with the ABiH army throughout the period of the war, which is, let's say, June 1992, December 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: You gave evidence that you spent around nine months, maybe less, deployed in the area of the Nisic plateau; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Where did you spend the rest of your services with the 115th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rest of the time I spent in the area of responsibility, in the city of Sarajevo between Kozija Cuprija up to Debelo Brdo, in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: So that we can say that in the period between 1992 and 1995, June 1992, December 1995, out of this whole period, you only spent nine months in Nisic and the rest of the period deployed in the Sarajevo -- in the city of Sarajevo area of responsibility, the 115th Brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can I ask the court officer please to call Rule 65 ter number 44, and I will call page 12 of the B/C/S/document and page 7 of the English document; and not to be broadcast, please. 65 ter 44; page 12 of the B/C/S and page 7 of the English translation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is this it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Looks like, yes. And I'm waiting for the English, page 7. Can we ensure that it's not broadcast, please. Yes. Well, I think the witness can answer the question. Yes, the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness, do you see that B/C/S document in your monitor? Do you need to be zoomed or that to be zoomed or can you see your name in that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you recall that you gave a statement to Bosnian authorities, the CSB of Sarajevo? Do you remember that, about the incident that we were talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did give a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Let me read you briefly what it says at the second paragraph: "The officer in charge states that on 24 December 1994 we interview," I skip the witness name; and at the bottom of the same paragraph, it says: "About the explosion of artillery projectiles at the flea market near the Vijecnica building on 22nd November, 1994 at around 0900 hours." Is that correct? December -- I'm sorry, 22nd December, 1994. Can you read it in the B/C/S document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of the second paragraph on the 22nd of December, 1994. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're asking the witness to say whether that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, primarily to recognise this as the statement that he gave to the Bosnian authorities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I tender this document into exhibit, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we admit it, under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number P309, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And I would actually tender only this page. It's -- as usual it's a large document. It's a 33-page English document. I will seek to tender the very one page which has been shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. What is admitted is the particular page shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: If I may, a final remark in terms of redaction. To be consistent with the decision this Honourable Chamber has made for the redaction of page 29 of today's transcript, I will refer your attention, Your Honours, to page 78, line 18 to -- lines 18 to 23 of yesterday's transcript where the same information of today were disclosed. So as a matter of consistency, I will ask the redaction of also that small portion of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you through now?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. President. That concludes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, during this trial, you are actually the first witness to appear who has ever seen the front line, and the Chamber is interested in knowing a little more about what the front line looked like. So my question is, if you could tell us a bit what was visible at the front lines. I understand that there were trenches, but were there trenches all along the front line, or was it just trenches some parts and other parts there would be nothing? That's one question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What did the front line look like in the urban areas? For instance, in the western side of your area of responsibility in Grbavica, how would the front line there be visible, and how was it manned? Were there soldiers on both sides looking at each other? And my third question would be in the rural areas in the hills, was the -- were the grounds between the two front lines, between the BiH army and the Republika Srpska army, were those areas there full of land-mines, or could you walk across them without any damage, I mean, except for the risk of being shot? Could you clarify a bit about what the front line looked like for the Chamber, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS W-12 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was like this, roughly speaking: Wherever it was possible to dig a trench, one tried to dig one, and to get as close as possible to the enemy lines precisely because of the shelling. The closer one got to them, the greater the possibility not to come under shelling, because in that case the enemy would have lay their own positions bare, expose them to the shelling. The trenches had connecting tunnels, connecting trenches. You didn't leave those because you would have exposed yourself to shelling and to bullets. That's what the line was like above Sarajevo, for the most part, in the Trebevic area which is where I was. As for other parts of Sarajevo, for the most part I didn't know exactly, but I think the lines mostly ran through buildings and basements and what have you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. The next witness is witness number 131, Mr. Ekrem Suljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may be excused please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sorry. While the witness is being brought in and we are trading places, if I could just steal a moment here to address that translation issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The issue pertains to Exhibit D19 which was discussed with the witness. Limiting myself strictly to the translation issue, and not the larger issue that it touches, we don't really have any comment on it. Looking back at the document, I think what happened is the Prosecution was looking at one paragraph of the document and the Defence was looking at another; and, in fact, the translation that's been provided is consistent with the translation which is in evidence with this exhibit. So we don't see any difficulty, and we don't really have any further comment on the translation issue as such. It's fine with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tapuskovic, any brief submissions on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any objections myself. I do, however, believe that it is my duty to draw your attention to our motion dated 26th of February, 2007, since this motion is related to this entire document; given the fact that Barry Hogan, an investigator of this Tribunal, on the 30th of January, 2001, once all of the evidence about this had been heard, obtained a document that runs counter to the previous medical document. I believe that to some extent, and it's difficult to find the right word, this challenges everything that the Prosecution has been doing so far. How is it possible, after all of this, for a document to turn up that is fully in contradiction to all the previous medical documents, or for that matter any evidence that we have so far heard?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I have seen the motion that you said you have filed. What does it seek?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't mean to tire you with this. We filed this on the 26th of February; you must have received it. It's all explained in that motion, and I would not like to tire you with this now, but if you could please study that motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We will be examining the motion and giving a ruling on it, although I am surprised that you -- that are you not in a position to say what it seeks, but we will deal with that shortly. Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am in a position to tell you that. That motion, we are saying that this document cannot be admitted under 92 bis. If the document is -- so that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's a matter we'll attend to. Thank you very much, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is one thing that I would like to ask you. Could I please be excused?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Sure, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please sit. And you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And can I inform the Chamber that this is a 92 ter witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Please state your full name, your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
