utterances.text: Ekrem Suljevic, the 1st of September 1959, the village of Gvosa [phoen] in Foca municipality. This is in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, do you remember on the 28th of February, 1996 providing a statement to investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor at the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you remember providing another statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 10th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do. I wouldn't remember the exact date but I think the year sounds right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, I will show them to you in a moment, which should make everything clear. Do you remember meeting me, roughly, two weeks ago in my office, where I gave you an opportunity to read through those statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you recall upon reading those statements that you made a number of amendments and corrections to those statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you remember that those corrections and amendments were contained in another information report, and you had an opportunity to review that report and you signed it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do remember signing it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And with those corrections and amendments made to your two statements, is it your evidence that those statements reflect an accurate and valid state of events, according to your knowledge and memory?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And if you were to be asked questions today in Court, would those answers that you give reflect the contents of those statements and the information report with the corrections?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 2968 -- 2968 be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, do you see a document on your right-hand -- on the left-hand side of the screen there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And do you see your signature there at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that the statement you gave on the 28th of February, 1996?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number P310.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: May I now ask for 65 ter 02969 to be broadcast, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, same questions: Do you see your signature on that document, and is that the statement that you gave on the 10th of March, 1997?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I offer that into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number P311.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And, lastly, can I ask that 65 ter 02970 be brought up?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, firstly, do you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Can we have the B/C/S version also on there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm told that the B/C/S version is page 3 and 4 of the same document. Can we just go to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, do you see your signature there at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is this document the corrections and amendments that you made to your two statements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that be admitted, as well, into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit number 312, P312.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, I'm just going to ask you a couple of questions, most of this is contained in your statements, but you worked for the Sarajevo KDZ during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. The KDZ was under the Republican Ministry of the Interior, which was based in the Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Was there another name for the KDZ that was commonly used?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Not really. Well, what this really means is counter-sabotage protection or bomb squad, if you like. That is what the department is called.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And what was your role within this department of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I was a pyrotechnics inspector at the time, all the way up until 1995, sometime in 1995, when I became the head of the pyrotechnics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you also undertake investigations into shelling incidents during the period 1994/1995, within that department?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do on-site investigations. I was involved with teams that carried out these investigations. I was in charge of analysing any evidence collected at crime sites, forensically.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you go to any on-site investigations with your team to conduct investigations within the sphere of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there were other people involved, too, so I didn't go to each and every on-site investigation. It depended. I sometimes did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you did go, did your responsibility, amongst other things, include analyses of craters and parts of projectiles that may have been found at the scene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Whenever I was there, I was supposed to help with crater analysis, in terms of establishing the direction of a projectile. I was also supposed to gather evidence, fragments of projectiles that exploded, which could then be used to conduct some sort of analysis in a lab, because this is the sort of the thing that you can't do at the actual site.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you conducted analysis of craters and determined the direction of fire, what -- well, let me put it this way: What sort of weaponry did you -- what kind of craters did you investigate? Were they craters from mortars, modified air bombs, other artillery projectiles? Could you describe that for the Court, please?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, depending on the projectile used, craters could vary. Very peculiar type of crater is that caused by a mortar shell, which is different from a crater produced by an artillery weapon. As to air bombs, these would normally be large holes. If, for example, a bomb hit the ground, or if it hit a building, what would be left would be a large-scale ruin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say "other artillery projectiles," could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Projectiles fired by artillery weapons. They rotate in flight as opposed to mortar shells. These actually rotate around their own axis during their flight.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know what a 76-millimetre shell is? What kind of weapon is that, or projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a shell that is fired by a 76-millimetre cannon. This projectile also revolves or rotates around its own axis during its flight, around its own axis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate range of such a projectile?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm no expert in that field; but based on our work, based on the requirements of our work, I am familiar with certain types of information. As with any other artillery projectile, or mortar shells for that matter, there are different kinds of charge; the more powerful the charge, the larger the range of a projectile. In this specific case, if you have a 76-millimetre gun, a cannon, there are four charges, one to four. And the most powerful charge normally implies that the range is, and I can't remember exactly, but I think it must have been over 8 kilometres; between 8 and 9 kilometres, that's what the rage would be. I'm talking about the charge number four, which is the most powerful charge possible for this type of projectile.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. I'm going to ask you a few questions about a particular incident in a moment; but, firstly, just generally, can you tell the Court when you conducted on-site investigations and when you analysed projectiles or parts of projectiles in your office at the KDZ, were reports and notes routinely made?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: On-site investigations were normally conducted by our colleagues from the Security Services Centre. Every time they submitted a request with evidence collected at a scene, fragments were, as a rule, analysed, fragments that were collected at the site of an explosion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you analyse these fragments, did you produce reports? Did your unit produce reports?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And given your time at the Ministry of the Interior at the KDZ, did you, during that period, have the occasion to -- to review or to read reports from other departments of the Ministry of the Interior? That is, CSB reports, official reports, on-site investigation reports, photographs -- official photo documentation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't get their reports or any other documents or any notes. If, for example, there was a judge present at an on-site investigation, we would receive a request for evidence or any fragments found at the scene to be analysed, do our job, and then we would send back our report containing any evidence that was found. So the evidence was, in a manner of speaking, sent right back to the Security Services Centre, and I think that sort of thing is still kept there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: If you had seen such reports during your time at the Ministry of the Interior, would you have been in a position to -- to recognise them as valid documents from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, do you remember when you first came on the 18th of February, and also this morning, that you were shown a series of official reports, photo documentation, maps, and other police documentation?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. One thing I don't remember is the date I arrived; the 18th or the 19th of February, I'm not sure. But I saw the documents then and I saw them this morning, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did you have the time to review those documents carefully?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Did you come to a conclusion as to the authenticity or the validity of these documents?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I found all the documents to be both valid and authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: After reviewing these documents, did you then review carefully a spreadsheet containing a list of the documents that you had previously seen?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: A spreadsheet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And after reviewing the spreadsheet carefully with the list of documents, did you sign that spreadsheet and date it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, could I ask that 65 ter 30 -- sorry, 03012 be brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. It's -- certainly, yes. I should say that I -- you don't need my permission to do that. It's your evidence that you are leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Actually, could we go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Suljevic, do you see your signature there?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that the spreadsheet containing the list of materials and documents that you reviewed carefully in my office?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And can you confirm to the Court that the materials and documents contained in this spreadsheet are authentic and valid documents from the Sarajevo CSB or Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, as the Prosecution has in the past done with witness 28 and Dr. Mandilovic, the Prosecution would like to tender into evidence the materials and the photographs contained in this spreadsheet as separate items of evidence, in addition to the spreadsheet, in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, let that be done. Ms. Isailovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As to the document under number 9, after reviewing, then I realise that these documents deal with an incident which was withdrawn from the list after your decision, which is bombing number or shelling incident number 4, the incident of December the 12th; and pursuant to your decision, the Prosecution should not tender documents into evidence regarding this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What you're saying is that we have excluded the presentation of evidence -- what you're saying is that we had in our 73 bis decision excluded the presentation of evidence on that incident. What incident is this on? Is that shelling incident number 4, you say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. That was a shelling that took place on the 12th of December, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I make a brief submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: My learned friend is absolutely right, and I can only apologise that it was an oversight. I believe that it is indeed an incident that was removed by Your Honours' ruling, and I can only say that I am constantly focussing on the incidents that we are dealing with, that it was an oversight, so I'm happy to remove that from the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, that's to be removed from the spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, these items will then be given Exhibit numbers 313 up to 326, following the numbers on the spreadsheet and with exception from item number 1 -- 9, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And may I also ask the spreadsheet to be admitted into evidence, barring, of course, item number 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this spreadsheet will be Exhibit number 327.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Mr. Sachdeva, let me put a question to the witness. Witness W-131, at some point in time you worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Hello, Witness. My name is Branislava Isailovic. I work for the Paris Bar Association, and I defend General Dragomir Milosevic, present in this courtroom, who is charged here by this Tribunal. I have a number of questions to put to you concerning your statement, which you discussed with the Prosecutor a while ago, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And, today, the Prosecutor told us that you made a few changes to your statements. Is that also true?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You made more changes to your first statement, i.e., the one that's dated 28th of February, 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, a certain number of changes were inserted.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In these statements, now I'm putting the question to you, do you need to have the statement on the screen. Even though you have looked at these this morning with the Prosecutor, would you like this to be displayed on the screen?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: If you think it's necessary, then it's all right with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, maybe it's a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These statements are not in e-court. We have not put these statements on our list. This is P310; that is his statement of the 28th of February, 1996. Can we turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: According to information provided a few weeks ago, you stated that you were a mechanical engineer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. Until a few weeks only. Since 1993, actually, I was a -- became a mechanical --

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in this statement, which was given in 1996, it is stated - maybe it's a mistake - it is stated that you were technology constructor. Two weeks ago, you made a change here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Due to some confusion in the interpretation, this change was input, but I can explain, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I shall pick up on this new piece of information you've given us. I reckon that this is right. Did you acquire your knowledge as a mechanical engineer in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 10th of January, 1983, I graduated from the Faculty of Mechanical Engineering in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: What you studied at the Mechanical Faculty in Sarajevo, did your training focus on anything pertaining to ammunition?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When did you acquire this knowledge which would entitle you to act as an expert on matters relating to ammunition?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, he is not here as an expert, which is a technical term in -- in the courts. We have a particular procedure for -- for experts and we're not following that procedure. It doesn't mean that he is not here to give evidence that relates to a specialised field, and you're perfectly entitled to test him as to his qualifications to give the kind of evidence that he is giving. But I just wanted to clarify that he is not here as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you for your remark. But I wanted to put the question to him because under domestic jurisdiction, he appeared to be an expert on craters.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, let me resume. The Security Services Centre in Sarajevo, you conducted crater analysis, is that right, is that the kind of thing you did?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Crater analysis were conducted on the spot. That's the trace in the ground left by the projectile. You cannot take it with you. It has to remain at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Did you yourself get involved in this kind of analyses, on the spot, I mean?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with a view to determining the direction from which a projectile came.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And when did you acquire that knowledge that would entitle you to conduct this kind of analysis?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This type of analysis doesn't require any specific knowledge. You just need practice; therefore, there is no training course for this kind of an analysis, teaching you how to do these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had no training in these matters?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: As I told you, it was based on practice, and you acquire a knowledge through practice. One didn't need any special training. It's not any specific science how you determine the direction of a projectile based on the shape and the features of the crater.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, and when did you start conducting crater analysis, when did you put this into practice?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Before 1993, I had been working at Zrak company, which was a special purpose factory in the former Yugoslavia. From November 1993, I started working at the KDZ department. Initially, I took part in on-site investigations and wasn't involved in expert analysis. I attended the scenes as a kind of an assistant; and throughout this period, I acquired this knowledge through practical work in the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can I infer from your previous answer that you established a connection between the job you were doing in the Zrak factory and the fact that you were able to analyse craters after that, and that you had a knack for it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. My job in -- in this company had nothing to do with projectiles and artillery weapons of any kind. My job in this company -- now we go back to the technologition [as interpreted], or someone who is involved in various technological processes, and I was a mechanical engineer. We were dealing with optical systems, guiding systems for anti-tank rockets, and we were developing these kind of systems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can I infer from this that the Zrak factory was an arms factory?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Zrak factory was what we call the special purpose industry in the former the Yugoslavia, for the former Yugoslavia People's Army. It manufactured optical devices and other devices, to be used among other things for certain weapons, and I myself wasn't involved in all those weapons. It was a huge range of products and optical devices used in an army; sighter devices, optical devices, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And as you left this factory in 1993 [Realtime transcript read in error "1983"], can I infer from that that this factory was under the control of the ABiH army after that?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1993, you mean, because you said in 1983. Between 1983 and 1993, I worked in this factory which is located in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you know, up until 1993 and thereafter, did the -- this factory still produce the same kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This factory is still in operation. I don't know what its capacity nowadays is, but it's still working. I mean, it's still in the same field. I don't believe that they still have the same range of products because there is no need for that, and they don't have the capacity to do that. I don't know. I didn't go to visit it for at least ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But during the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and from 1992 onwards, did this factory remain under the control of the ABiH army; namely, from 1992 up until the -- up until the Dayton agreement. Is that right? Agreements?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's based in Sarajevo, and the factory was never occupied.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that throughout the entire conflict, it was still manufacturing armament for the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This factory operated throughout the war with a very reduced capacity of output.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you left this factory in 1993, and when did you start conducting crater analyses?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This department was involved in this particular area; and since I joined the department, I started becoming -- started to familiarise myself with what they were doing, starting with the landing of projectiles, et cetera, and I continued to do that until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I would like to put the name of one of his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we could move into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, I'd like to refer to page 3 of your statement in both versions, because we already have one of the versions on the screen, so the B/C/S version, please. We don't have paragraphs here, but it's paragraph 9 as a matter of fact, and it's starting with [B/C/S spoken] "in which I was involved." In the English version, "I was also involved." It's the fourth paragraph in the sheet. I derived from that paragraph that you establish or you established special relationships for the purposes of your evidence today at this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No. The first time I got in touch with anyone from the International Tribunal was back in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, this wasn't my question. My question -- perhaps I'll read this paragraph, [In English] "which hit the flea market on 22 December 1994. The report which you have shown me, signed by [French spoken], is an example of the brief reports we wrote prior to the knowledge that the Tribunal was interested in our work." So my question is as follows: You started writing reports because you wanted to use them for the Tribunal, and the fact that you started writing for the Tribunal meant that you wrote the reports differently. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Up to that point, we had been compiling reports, and we had been asked to analyse countless missiles falling on the city of Sarajevo, regardless of whether these missiles landed somewhere among the houses, in a garden, for example, without necessarily injuring anyone. There were too many of these missile and too many of these incidents. Sometimes we would receive several requests in a single day. The reports had to be concise. The point being to identify the projectiles without being too competent assist. You see that there are no specific descriptions very often, but what we looked for were telltale signs that could help us to identify the type of projectile that was used. The scope of our work was reduced later on. We only carried out on-site investigations when there were casualties; people wounded or killed. There was no point in us going out all the time. There were thousands and thousands of missiles falling on the city every day. It would have taken many more people to do that sort of job.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Reading your statement, I come to the conclusion that the report you wrote after the 22nd of December incident on the flea market belongs to this category of brief reports, which were drafted before you started writing reports for the ICTY. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's a brief report. You can tell by just looking at it. The one thing that is unequivocal is the final opinion on what was established; how the projectile was identified, the one that exploded in that particular location. There were two at that particular market, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And for this report, did you go on the spot? Did you visit the scene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, I did go to the scene of the explosion after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You have just stated that the type of weaponry used was clear and unambiguous, according to your analysis?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. It was based on the mark left by the missile or the crater, based on the fragments found at the scene. We realised this was a 76-millimetre missile that had been fired by a gun, a cannon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember UNPROFOR forces being present on the scene during your investigations?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: UNPROFOR arrived at the scene. I can't say when exactly, but they followed us. We were there by the time they arrived. Speaking of this incident, their investigation of the direction was independent, and then we would cross reference our results and our results tallied. We arrived -- we had arrived at the same result, which they subsequently confirmed. Our conclusions were identical, and the direction that had been established appeared to be accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember the conclusion of UNPROFOR on the weapon used?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the conclusion, but last week when I arrived here, I eventually saw their report and I don't agree with what it says about these having been mortar shells. When I saw for the first time that that was what their report stated, that those had probably been mortar shells that had been used, I disagreed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I understand, the Prosecutor has shown you these UNPROFOR conclusions.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Well, then, I'm sorry to say that these conclusions were not disclosed to us, because in our documents we have several UN documents missing. Since it is difficult for to us to lay our hands on them, I have here with me something which was disclosed, which is Mr. Angatsori's [phoen] statement, who's an UNPROFOR member, his statement for the purposes of witness evidence here. Unfortunately, he is not a witness in this particular case, but it is a statement to the Office of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since it is not present in e-court, I have prepared paper copies of that document which I'll ask the usher to circulate it. It is in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But you, Witness, are already aware of this, because it actually confirms what you have just stated. So we are talking about Mr. Angatsori; his name is mentioned in the report as having been involved in the investigation, which was conducted parallelly to the Bosnian police's investigation. Witness, my question is as follows: You came to the unambiguous conclusion to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: You came to an ambiguous conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: And your conclusion was different from UNPROFOR's conclusions. My question is as following: After performing the analysis, have you looked into the possibility of other possible conclusions on the same facts?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: When we finished our analysis, we drew up a report. This report was compiled based on the fragments found at the scene. These fragments come from a 75-millimetre projectile. No stabilising fins were found such as normally found in mortar shells, something that would have indicated the use of a mortar shell. I'm not sure what UNPROFOR based their opinion on. This was an independent report that they made later on. I do know that while there, we cross-referenced the directions that we had measured and our results tallied at the time. That's all can I tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you have compared the direction, but have you also calculated the distance from which the shell was fired?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, earlier on, you talked about different charges for a gun shell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But that is only the extent of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Would you consider yourself as an expert in gun shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what exactly you mean when you say, "an expert in gun shells."

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Are you positive that there can be different charges for gun shells?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: This is not in reference to the projectile but the propulsion charge. The more powerful the propulsion, the farther a projectile is likely to fly. A shell is just a shell. There is just a single type of shell. No aberrations. It always has a certain type of charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we are talking about the same thing, about the propelling charge. This is what you had in mind, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's right, the propulsion charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: You have just said that you haven't found -- that you didn't find the stabilising fins on the scene on the 22nd of December. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The fins would have indicated that a mortar shell had been used. The projectiles fired from a gun have no fins. It's the rotation that gives them a certain trajectory and a certain stability in their flight. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When analysing craters, have you already come across an instance in which the stabilising fins vanished from the scene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I did a number of on-site investigations, and whenever we were dealing with a mortar shell, fins were invariably found. I don't know what became of those later on. I'm not going into that. This would be submitted to us for analysis and then returned for further analysis perhaps. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So one important part of your analysis was the absence of the stabilising fins, and is this one of the main things you base this on to conclude that the shell had been fired by a 76-millimetre gun?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't call it that important. When you conduct an analysis, you need to take into consideration all the fragments that you retrieve. It is based on all the fragments that you establish that, not based on what is not there. There are these fragments that are submitted for analysis. You will find some of our reports where we were simply unable to ascertain, based on the fragments received, what the projectile was that had been used. And then the conclusion would be, based on the evidence submitted, it is impossible to identify the projectile used.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the very fragments, on the basis of the same fragments, your analysis and UNPROFOR's analysis diverged; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, our report clearly states that the fragments belonged to a 76-millimetre shell. The UNPROFOR report states that this was probably a mortar shell. I don't know what they based their finding on. I know what we based on conclusion on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In the final paragraph of your statement - and part of your statement has been amended, so please do take these amendments into account - but in the final paragraph of your statement you mention this 22nd of December incident and you talk about the existence of the buildings which may have been a basis for your analysis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. There are no buildings there that would make it possible what the angle of descent was of that particular projectile. It was impossible to conclude whether it was at a lower angle or a higher angle. I'm not sure if I'm making any sense. If you have this cannon, the same charge, you can have two different angles. You can use two different angles and still have the projectile land in the same place, depending on where the weapon is positioned. It can be positioned in a protected place. It can be used to fire from behind a hill, for example. You have lower angles; you have higher angles. My knowledge of this field is only modest. But for a projectile to land one and the same place, you could actually fire it from two different angles, if using that kind of weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So when performing your 22nd of December, 1994 analysis, all these elements were missing.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by "elements were missing." The direction of the missile was ascertained beyond any doubt at all. There's always some symmetry. If you look at the marks left by a missile, this is always at the mercy of the elements, the weather, that sort of thing. There's always some degree of aberration that is taken into account. Plus or minus 5 or 10 degrees, the direction was established. What we weren't able to establish we simply didn't record. It was on the spot that we ascertained the direction. We collected the evidence based on whatever evidence was collected. An analysis was drawn up and the projectile was identified. You can identify a projectile based on the fragments found. Sometimes these fragments were marked. Each projectile is marked in a certain way. Sometimes these markings were found or bits of these markings. Sometimes there were fins. So based on that, you establish what the calibre was and what the type of shell was that was used.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on you said that there were many shells fired and many explosions in Sarajevo. I was wondering whether you were also looking at the presence of other shells on the scene?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Those two are theoretical possibilities. But you would collect evidence around a crater. A projectile comes flying in and then you can get different types of fragments or evidence. As far as I know, this sort of matter, material, is susceptible to corrosion. So even if you come there the next day, you're likely to find that the fragments had been altered by natural corrosion.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: When you were thinking and analysing, did you also take into account the injuries of the victims?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Most often there were no casualties. Once we arrived at the scene, everybody had already been taken to hospital. There was no point for to us wait there to carry out an investigation while people are being removed. Therefore, there were very few occasions where I arrived at the scene while there were still some casualties there. But basically I never found anyone at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, Witness, would you agree that the nature and kind of wound would indicate where the shot came from?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. After an explosion, who is capable of determining how the victim was standing and where he or she was standing? And I don't think that's the basis for establishing the direction of a projectile.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall get back to this affidavit which the Prosecutor has submitted and which the Chamber has just tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In these documents, there is a whole series of medical reports which you have reviewed today, and you have, under oath, stated that these are true to fact.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that they are authentic. As for the contents thereof, I had never seen it before, nor did I write it. But the documents, as documents, are authentic, produced by authorised or organs or institutions. I didn't go into the contents thereof; what kind of injuries were sustained, who were the victims, et cetera. It is not up to me to evaluate that because I don't know what happened on the spot. That is why I just say, "Yes, for example, there was this and this casualty." And I think that these documents are authentic because they are based on actual events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, if my learned friend is talking about the spreadsheet, there is no mention of medical reports being shown to the witness or at least being -- at least contained in this spreadsheet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To substantiate what I have just said, I'm dealing with document 8, for instance. This is a 65 ter document, number 1340, and in these documents there are a series of medical reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if you look at number 8, can you see this? Did you see this today? You haven't seen a single medical report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Where does it say it's medical, Ms. Isailovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have received the list of documents which are in e-court, so I have retrieved the documents which are mentioned on the list. Number 8, for instance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I understand where the confusion lies. The documents on the spreadsheet are the ones that the witness has confirmed, and if you look at -- if Your Honours look at item 8, it is indeed from 65 ter 1340; however, it's clearly indicated that only pages 5 to 7 of that composite case file were shown to the witness. That was the official report for incident 21st June 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is admitted is confined to pages 5 to 7?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And on e-court the full range is obviously contained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So there you have it, Ms. Isailovic. It's only pages 5 to 7 that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I stand to be corrected, but I shall get back to this affidavit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot confirm any medical report in your affidavit?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot -- I'm not capable of confirming a medical report at all. If I see a document, I can only say whether it is authentic, whether it has been issued by an authorised institution. I cannot confirm the contents or the veracity thereof. I'm not an expert there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But are there medical reports in his, what you call, affidavit? Are there medical reports in his affidavit?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was not feeling very well this morning; that's why I came in late this morning. In the meantime, we had three lists, and this was something that we greed with the Prosecution. I was unable to write down the numbers this morning and my case file was prepared last night for today. This case file contains these reports, but if it's redacted, it's even better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sachdeva, are there medical reports in the statements that were admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: No. I mean, that's why the pages are indicated. And, in fact, the specific ERNs from the B/C/S versions, the original versions, are clearly marked. I didn't show the witness medical reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Right. So you shouldn't ask the question: So you cannot confirm any medical report in your affidavit, because we already settled that there aren't any. So proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement - I don't have it on my screen anymore; could it be put up on the screen, please; this is Exhibit P310 - you did talk about specific cases which you were able to talk about, given that you had taken part in the investigations. The incident that occurred on the 28th of June, 1995, when an air bomb had fallen on the television building, do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I visited the scene and carried out the on-site investigation of this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Do not look at the document you have on your screen because the numbers have been switched around. This is the document now. Page 3. You say in your statement that when you reached the site you found no fragments.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that's not correct. I don't know where you found that, that no shrapnel was found.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you could correct what's written in here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I see. The question that you put to him was that in his statement -- you say that when he reached the site, he found no fragments, and then he answered: "That's not correct. I don't know where you found that, that no shrapnel was found." I'm not sure whether there is a distinction being made between fragments and shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, there shouldn't be any distinction between fragments and shrapnel. It is it possible, though, that this statement refers to the fact that in this incident there were no remnants of the engine found, of the rocket engine, which was an integral part of this modified air bomb. But shrapnel were found and that's what I put in our report subsequent to our analysis. And you will see there that we examined each and every piece of shrapnel that we found at the scene.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, you didn't find any rocket or engine fragments on the site; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: But, nonetheless, you did conclude that it must have been an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: EKREM SULJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Isailovic, in view of the fact that are you not well, and the Chamber has observed that, we'll take the adjournment now.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISAILOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness, you may leave, to return on Monday at 9.00. In the intervening time, you are not to discuss your evidence with anybody, and that includes the Prosecution. Please take the witness out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of March, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
